INTRODUCTION Pipeline networks can experience component failure when subjected to extreme pressure loadings, such as those prevalent in a nuclear blast. Of key interest to planners is how much damage can be expected given a specific blast scenario. Pipeline networks are necessarily complex structures, with many significant details present in pipe connections and distribution centers, to name but a few. This complexity can complicate assessment of pipeline failure under load. However, a general understanding of pipeline status post-blast can be found by simply considering the failure of the pipes themselves. Pipe collapse within a network segment affects the rest of the system and is generally time- and cost-intensive to repair. Pipe collapse is a reasonably complex physical process, involving the interactions of a range of factors such as pipe geometry, pipe strength, pipeline support distance, and, for buried pipes, depth of burial and soil properties. For pipeline designers, simplified design expressions provide a mechanism to address this complexity through easy computation of collapse pressures. While designers use these to ensure that their pipelines will maintain integrity through expected applied loads, these design expressions can also be used to approximate whether the pipes will fail under applied pressure loads. This report identifies several useful design expressions found in the pipeline design literature and defines the needed inputs to compute collapse pressures for several failure mechanisms. A set of representative pipe definitions, along with a set of representative nuclear blast loads, demonstrate the use of these expressions to assess pipe failure in relevant environments. Finally, variation of key parameters in these expressions illustrate how changes in design parameters affect pipeline survivability. 8 2. EXPRESSIONS FOR PIPELINE COLLAPSE DUE TO APPLIED PRESSURE To be able to provide an easily computable failure pressure for a given pipeline, this work started with a survey of pipeline design literature [1-7]. Reference [4] included a detailed analysis of structural design considerations for pipelines and had the largest range of applicable expressions. Most of the expressions detailed below are derived from this source. Both above- and below-ground expressions are considered. 2.1. Yielding due to external pressure Yielding of the pipe cross section under external load is the most straightforward of the failure criteria considered; failure occurs when the applied external pressure exceeds both the internal pressure and yield stress of pipe material. This would result in yielding of the steel throughout the cross section of the pipe. Assuming minimal hardening of the material post-yield (a reasonable assumption for pipe steel), collapse would then be imminent given any non-symmetry in the loading.
